Magazine hunting quickly became a ritual. Every pay- check became an excuse to convince my older brother to drive us to our local Barnes & Noble, where I would nearly empty my wallet moments after walking through the doors. At the time, I had no intention of starting a magazine. I was content being a connoisseur—absorbing writing on our collective social, political climates; indulging artists’ processes; gathering fashion inspiration; and lin- gering over photography that honored its subjects as much as their image. When I ﬁ rst entertained the idea of turning my notebook into a magazine, I imagined I’d have time for it decades later. Arbitrary, but it made sense to me then. I put a pin in the idea as I ﬁ nished college, though I continued ﬁ lling the journal’s pages, committed to being as honest as pos- sible in my writing. As life would have it, I spent the next two and a half years bouncing around the East Coast, still collecting expe- riences in that same notebook whenever I could spare moments between countless odd jobs, befriending won- derful people, evading predatory landlords, trying to make space for creative work, and the occasional lover. Most of the time, I was more focused on balancing responsibili- ties than giving my creative ideas consistent attention. I let life carry me forward until a brief affair in the fall of 2024 became a quiet wake-up call. By the time it ended the fol- lowing spring, 2025, I found myself returning to passions I had slowly drifted away from, and the magazine came back into focus. Though my life grew busier than ever as I took on a second job to make ends meet, I settled into a peaceful but demanding rhythm I hadn’t experienced before. With less free time, I began cutting away what no longer served me, focusing instead on what mattered most. That summer, I began work on my recording project, I REMEMBER THE moment BULLET ﬁ rst slipped out from Eidah. shoes on indoors
STYLED BY KONNIE RENE SHOT BY ISAIAH ARTESE
“This project was simply a way to play dress up with my friends.”
Shot entirely in our apartment in North Philadelphia.
Styling is something I recently got into, starting in the spring of 2025. When dressing myself, I’ve always noticed parallels between storytelling and clothing—the nuances in what clothes say about an individual, a moment in time, and the state of the world. Upon moving to Philly, I had the idea of building an archive of clothing as a way to help others tell those same stories intentionally through dress.
Styling—like music, design, and the other creative mediums I move through—is a way for me to take agency over my own story, while also drawing cultural and spiritual connections to the world around me. I often ﬁ nd myself thinking about how identity is layered and inherited and shifts across place.
In that way, this project naturally carries motifs of Afro-Caribbean and Afro-diasporic expression alongside European, American, and Asian styles—putting them in conversation. Poet shirts meet knit tights and lace; culottes, scarves, durags, and vintage U.S. Navy pants exist in the same frame. These references aren’t meant as separation, but as overlap—the way culture actually lives in people rather than in categories. The clothing worn by the models—and myself—becomes a kind of gateway: into not just my own story and ancestry, but also into the lives and inﬂ uences I’ve encountered since moving to Philadelphia and building community here.
—Konnie Rene

I STOPPED USING streaming services a year and a half ago when I realized that not only did I not even enjoy the service I was paying for, but no one was making me stay. I remembered that I didn’t have to use any platforms to listen to music, I could get it straight from the source. I googled the newest ways to download music “legally”, found a method that didn’t seem too labor intensive, and cancelled my Spotify subscription. (I also bought an iPod on Ebay, but that’s besides the point.) I missed having to actually ﬁ nd music. I missed the effort it takes, having to download an album three different times because I got the wrong versions. I missed owning my music. I like down- loading an album I’ve never heard by an artist I don’t know, and falling in love with a world that I never knew existed. I like that I don’t need to have cell service to listen to it. Spotify, and all of its conveniences, has killed connection. Spotify’s worst crime is convincing us that we do indeed need it. Whenever I have to tell someone how I listen to music, I’m often met with confusion. “How do you listen, then,” they may say, as if we are forced to give a company money to even get access. Spotify, and the rest of the streaming world, have done such a good job at integrating themselves into people’s lives that they’ve erased the possibility of a world without them. The polished, stream- lined algorithms of Spotify make any other method seem tedious in comparison. The real issue here is that Ek saw piracy as a problem to solve, rather than a symptom of a bigger issue that he and his company are complicit in perpetuating. I think back to LimeWire, Napster, and even the newer tools that I use today, and I know that piracy has never been about theft, but autonomy and assuming control over the art that we consume. In a world where we have access to everything but own nothing, those small acts feel radical. Art isn’t something that we interact with any- more, but something to scroll past and forget about. Own- ership makes music deliberate. It makes it matter. Every time we press play on a “daylist” named some- thing like “twang slacker rock wednesday early morning”, we take another step towards passivity.
